translations: Zhu Yingtai corrected herself, "We didn't fall into the water."
Aman said, "That's even more worth remembering, showing that both of them passed the exam."

Liang Shanbo invited him to walk together, but Aman only followed him to the academy's gate, confirming they arrived safely, before continuing on his own path, never once seeing through Zhu Yingtai's disguise.

Inside the academy, Zhu Yingtai faced a new challenge: she had to be careful with her living arrangements, bathing, and daily interactions. She proposed to the academy's administrators that she sleep lightly, and asked to be assigned a room near the outside; she also volunteered to take morning water duties, so their schedules wouldn't conflict. Liang Shanbo thought she was just being particular, and helped her move books, but never once peeked inside.

While moving books, the door to the small room near the outside had a skewed hinge, and when pushed, it would swing back shut, trapping Liang Shanbo's sleeve. He didn't dare let go of the books, so he stood there half-turned, saying, "Zhu brother, this room is very good at keeping guests." Zhu Yingtai put down her own bag, took the top stack of books from him, and then helped him open the door.

After checking, they found that the door hinge was missing a piece of wood. Zhu Yingtai found a thin piece of wood, and Liang Shanbo helped her lift the door. The first time, the wood was too thick, and the door wouldn't close; the second time, it was too thin, and the door creaked loudly when closed. The neighbors thought someone was sawing wood inside, and Liang Shanbo replied, "The door is reciting its entrance speech, the sentences are a bit long."

Zhu Yingtai suppressed a smile, and changed the direction of the wood, then applied some wax to the hinge. The door finally opened and closed quietly, and could be securely locked from the inside. This small repair gave her a private space to herself. Liang Shanbo didn't take the opportunity to peek inside her still-unpacked trunk, but instead asked if the bookshelf needed to be raised to prevent water damage.

That evening, the administrator came to check on the new students' living arrangements. The door latch was locked from the inside, and Zhu Yingtai answered the knock, then opened the door, her clothes neatly arranged. The administrator saw only books, bedding, and a repaired old door hinge, and didn't ask any further questions. As soon as the administrator left, Zhu Yingtai realized she had put her shoes on the wrong feet. She sat on the bed, changing her shoes, and Liang Shanbo, outside, heard the noise and asked if he could help.
"No need, I'm just discussing the direction with my shoes," Zhu Yingtai replied.

Liang Shanbo replied seriously, "If you can't agree, you could mark the direction with a note on the shoe tip." The next day, he brought her two small pieces of colored fabric, saying they could be sewn inside to help her identify which shoe was which. Zhu Yingtai took the fabric, feeling both that he was being genuinely helpful and that it was a rare kind of help that didn't pry into her secrets. She didn't tell him why she had put her shoes on the wrong feet the night before, but sewed one piece into her shoe and kept the other in her book bag.

As time passed, the two formed a routine: Liang Shanbo would block unnecessary visitors, and Zhu Yingtai would take care of morning water duties and tidy up the shared study area. Neither of them turned their help into a way to pry into each other's secrets. Her true identity remained safe, but she gained the freedom to continue studying thanks to the specific details of the door latch, their schedules, and their mutual respect.

The first night, a neighbor came to borrow a lamp and tried to push open the door. Liang Shanbo blocked the door, saying the new student was still unpacking and didn't need to check on them. He also moved his own bed to the outside, so that anyone entering or leaving would have to pass by him first. Zhu Yingtai thus avoided many hasty cover-ups, and simply appreciated his consideration.

Liang Shanbo noticed that she never wanted to join the others for a bath by the river, and asked if she was afraid of water. Zhu Yingtai looked at him, saying, "Liang brother asks this question, the bridge probably has different opinions." Liang Shanbo thought for a moment, then decided not to press the issue.

In the first exam, the teacher asked the new students to explain a passage. Zhu Yingtai gave a precise explanation, and Liang Shanbo provided simple examples to support her points. Their answers complemented each other, and the teacher assigned them to sit together. From then on, they studied together.

After class, Liang Shanbo said that they had been walking together and studying together, like fate. Zhu Yingtai replied, "If Liang brother doesn't put his ink in his sleeve next time, this fate might not have to wash one more piece of clothing."
Liang Shanbo looked down, and saw that his sleeve was already stained with ink. He apologized sincerely, as if Zhu Yingtai had saved a valuable manuscript.

From then on, the two became like brothers, officially becoming study partners. Liang Shanbo admired Zhu Yingtai's learning, thinking of her as a young, refined, and careful scholar, without suspecting her true identity. Their bond began with protecting the same book, walking across the same bridge, and sitting together at the same desk.
Their days together weren't just spent at the desk.

When the teacher explained a passage, Liang Shanbo was good at applying the principles to everyday life, while Zhu Yingtai could find three layers of meaning in a single sentence. They often argued over the meaning of a single character, but eventually combined their ideas to form a more complete answer.

Aman sometimes helped the academy by copying out their discussions. One time, while they were arguing over the phrase "heart as straight as the academy's bamboo poles," Zhu Yingtai raised her pen, a hint of teasing in her eyes, and said, "Liang brother, if our hearts were really like bamboo poles, wouldn't they sway in the wind, making it hard to stand firm?" Liang Shanbo didn't back down, looking out the window at the slanting sun, and replied, "At least bamboo poles can support a clothesline, even in strong winds and heavy rain, they can still hold the clothes steady." Aman, watching from the side, thought to himself, "These two are really using bamboo poles as a metaphor for philosophy." He copied out the phrase, with a neat hand, but added a playful "ya" after the word "bamboo," making it look even more playful. He then rewrote the sentence, saying, "Zhu brother praised Liang brother's usefulness, and Liang brother happily accepted." After finishing, Aman put down his pen, looked out the window, and thought to himself, "Their argument is both philosophical and amusing." Zhu Yingtai read the record and said, "We were just arguing." She smiled at Aman, and Aman nodded slightly, thinking to himself, "This record is both a collision of ideas and a moment of laughter."
Zhu Yingtai read the record and said, "We were just arguing."
Aman turned the bamboo slips over and said, "Our mutual respect is written all over the front, so we have to write our disagreements on the back."

The next moment, the teacher asked them to go take care of a sick classmate. Liang Shanbo stayed up late making medicine, while Zhu Yingtai organized the classmate's notes, so that when the classmate recovered, they wouldn't fall behind in their studies. The two worked together naturally, and Aman only noted that they had delivered medicine a few times.

When the classmate woke up, they saw a bowl of medicine, a stack of notes, and a bowl of already-cooled porridge on the bedside table. They asked who had worked the hardest, and Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai pointed to each other, their hands meeting in mid-air. The classmate sighed, "I was just feverish, but you two turned humility into a medicine."

One day, a strong wind blew open the window of the library, and rainwater was about to pour in. Zhu Yingtai moved the low bookshelves first, and Liang Shanbo climbed up to close the window. They worked until late at night, saving most of the books. Liang Shanbo's hand was cut by a splinter, and Zhu Yingtai carefully cleaned and bandaged it. Liang Shanbo just said that Zhu brother was more considerate than his own sister.
Zhu Yingtai asked, "If you had a sister like that, would you want to talk to her more?"
"Of course I would."
"If she also loved to read?"
"Then it would be even better. I could ask her all the questions I don't understand."

Zhu Yingtai looked at him, seeing that he was sincere, but still didn't catch the underlying meaning, and could only say, "Liang brother, when you get married, you should bring a wife who can listen to your secrets."
Aman was about to write "you need to bring a translator" but Zhu Yingtai glared at him, and he erased the word.

As time passed, the two became more familiar with each other. Liang Shanbo knew that Zhu Yingtai was afraid of the cold, and would leave a spot near the fire for her; Zhu Yingtai knew that Liang Shanbo was frugal, and would often borrow from him under the guise of discussing books. Liang Shanbo thought of these as brotherly gestures, but Zhu Yingtai realized that her feelings for him went beyond just being study partners.

In the winter, the academy ran out of coal, and Liang Shanbo moved his coal brazier between the two desks, saying, "One brazier can warm up two books, and learning will be warmer too." Zhu Yingtai knew he was doing it to keep her warm, but didn't expose him, and instead put her newly copied notes on his desk. They no longer needed to explicitly ask for each other's help, and it was precisely this that made their eventual parting more meaningful.
